items.body: The latest installment in the Portraits GRM series pairs the duo of crys cole & Oren Ambarchi with Italian maestro Giuseppe Ielasi. Each occupying a full side of vinyl, the result is a document of where contemporary sound practice finds itself in 2026 while paying homage to the institutional framework that made such work possible. This is not musique concrète in the traditional sense, but it is undeniably born from the same spirit of inquiry that drove Pierre Schaeffer to upend our relationship with sound nearly eighty years ago. Pierre Schaeffer (1910-1995) is remembered not necessarily for his music, or even his philosophical contributions to the study of sound (which were significant), but for his institution building. After pioneering musique concrète while working in French radio in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Schaeffer began almost instantly institutionalizing his legacy, what became the Groupe de Recherches Musicales (GRM) in 1958 (known as Ina-GRM since 1975). The tension between preserving a tradition and remaining open to the new has defined the institution ever since. My 2019 interview with François J. Bonnet—composer, philosopher, and current director of Ina-GRM—explored precisely this question: how does an institution honor its past while making space for the unfamiliar? An answer arrived in 2020 with the launch of Portraits GRM, a series of commissioned releases designed to bring contemporary voices into the GRM’s hallowed studios. The first release was Jim O’Rourke’s Shutting Down Here, fittingly so, as his sessions there spanned 30 years and thus that work’s completion constituted the closing of a significant loop. The re-issuing of classic and adjacent GRM titles began under the direction of Editions Mego, but after the death of Peter Rehberg (Pita) in 2021, the series transitioned to the stewardship of Shelter Press. Since then, Portraits GRM has featured Lucy Railton, Okkyung Lee, Kali Malone, Lasse Marhaug, Laurel Halo, Beatrice Dillon, and many others—artists who share little aesthetically but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do. As with most installments in the series, the latest release offers two compelling sidelong works from heavyweights of the experimental underground. On one side, crys cole and Oren Ambarchi continue their collaborative exploration of texture and density; on the other, Giuseppe Ielasi presents something distinctly his own. crys cole & Oren Ambarchi ~ Sparkling or Silent The title suggests something binary—a flickering between presence and absence, articulation and withholding—but the piece itself operates in the spaces between. Sparkling or Silent opens with what might best be described as ASMR-concrète: close-mic’d rustling, breath, the micro-articulations of objects manipulated in near-silence. It is intimate yet abstract, as though the listener has stumbled upon a private ritual. Over its 19’43’’ duration, the work unfolds in several distinct movements, each building upon the last until the accumulated density becomes something else entirely. Oren Ambarchi needs little introduction. The Australian guitarist has built a formidable reputation as a solo artist and one of the most prolific collaborators in experimental music, with a discography that touches on everything from the glacial drone of his solo work to the rhythmic propulsion of his trio with Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin—whose Ghosted series has only grown more assured with each installment. Records including Grapes from the estate (2004), Hubris (2016), and Simian Angel (2019) are personal favorites, not to mention his ongoing dialogues with figures like Keiji Haino and Jim O’Rourke. But alongside this celebrated career, there exists another body of work, equally significant if less discussed: his partnership with crys cole. Likely the less familiar name to many listeners, cole’s work is no less deserving of attention. I have been a fan of this Canadian sound artist’s practice for years, both in her solo work and her collaborations. Her third album for Black Truffle, Making Conversation collects three recent commissioned pieces and demonstrates a trajectory that has moved steadily toward greater formal control without sacrificing the tactile, almost sculptural quality of her sound. She had been involved with Winnipeg’s send + receive festival for over a decade, contributed photographs and projections to classic Canadian experimental records, and continues to be an active performer and sound artist. Her work with Ora Clementi—the duo with James Rushford—offers a dense thicket of sonic material that feels both organic and constructed. Sylva Sylvarum, in particular, stands as a high-water mark in her collaborative output. On Ambarchi’s Audience of One (2012), she’s credited as contributing contact microphones and brushes to the track “Passage.” They’ve since produced several records as a duo: Sonja Henies Vei 31 (2014), a hazy collage of intimate gesture and field recordings from a Norwegian sojourn; Hotel Record (2017), its title a dryly witty reference to its origins in hotel room sessions, a study in digital textures; and Gallivant (2021), documenting a live concert from the previous year. The pair have often played with others, including Keith Rowe and Leif Elggren. The collaborative dynamic is worth dwelling on, if only because there is something peculiar and generative about a musical duo that is also a romantic couple. One thinks of the historical precedents: Sonny and Linda Sharrock, whose volatile partnership produced some of the most ferocious free jazz of the late 1960s and early 1970s; Max Roach and Abby Lincoln, whose work together addressed civil rights with a moral urgency that still resonates, again overshadowed by a documented history of abuse. More recently, and hopefully less problematically, I think of Christina Vantzou and John Also Bennett, Matmos (MC Schmidt and Drew Daniel), and Two-Way Street—Ashlee Booth on cello and Adam Lion on percussion, for whom Sarah Hennies wrote a piece exploring precicely the dynamic between a romantic and musical partnership. Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe have even released a few short pieces as Eselsohr. There is something about the intimacy of shared life that translates into the shared space of improvisation and composition, a trust that allows for risk without the safety net of distance. A residency abroad, a portrait of two artists developing a shared vocabulary in confined spaces, the energy of a live recording. Sparkling or Silent represents something different—a consciously composed concert work. As the Portraits GRM materials describe it, the piece is “a moment apart in their respective artistic approaches” where an electroacoustic method that has always been latent in both of their practices “here asserts itself as a central compositional modality.” This shift from documentation to composition makes Sparkling or Silent feel more expansive and considered, even if it doesn’t necessarily represent a linear “evolution” so much as a deliberate side-step into a different mode of working. From its intimate opening, Sparkling or Silent gradually accumulates tonal densisty before dissolving again. About halfway through, after cohering into a sustained drone cloud, the texture thins; ghostly melodies and gentle rustlings emerge from the haze, while field recordings slowly ground us in an unexpected place. The real surprise arrives in the final four minutes: a sudden chorus of truck (?) horn harmonies. The effect recalls Alvin Curran’s Maritime Rites, transposed from water to asphalt; the collective ritual of Curran’s foghorns replaced by the found sounds of the highway. Within a minute, these sounds accumulate into a dense, surprisingly consonant cluster, overlapping blares forming a sustained fog of noise that continues until, finally, the sparkle turns to silence. It is a closing gesture that reframes everything that came before, revealing the delicate rustlings of the opening as part of a larger soundscape that extends far beyond the studio walls. The piece does not so much end as disperse, its constituent parts returning to the world from which they were borrowed.   Giuseppe Ielasi ~ unfamiliar music (paris) In Milano in 2017, I met Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe for dinner accompanied by Oren and crys, who were part-time residents of the city then—their European headquarters, before relocating to Berlin, was this underrated Italian metropolis, a base between their Australian and Canadian homelands. So in my mind, the connection between the artists featured on this record is obvious, forged not only through shared aesthetics but through shared meals, shared cities, shared lives. But Ielasi’s relationship to this series extends far beyond personal connections. He has mastered every Portraits GRM record except the first, and his own Senufo label released early records by Kassel Jaeger, which was in fact my introduction to François J. Bonnet many years ago. This record, then, feels like a culmination; the current director of Ina-GRM, the mastering engineer, the series, and the artists all intertwined in a web of mutual influence and respect that spans decades. Ielasi’s catalog is deep and varied, marked by a restless curiosity that refuses to settle into comfortable routines. He has his interests and proclivities—a fascination with small sounds, repetition, motors, unusual rhythmic grooves, in other words “an insistence on material”—but he rarely deploys the same technical setup or approach twice, constantly searching for new means of expression. This commitment to renewal is evident throughout his discography, from his early work on the 12k label to his more recent return to explorations of guitar and electronics. unfamiliar music (paris) arrives with some precedent. Ielasi has performed at the GRM before; I have a recording from 20 January 2014 at GRM Paris that captures his take on acousmatic diffusion. The title itself is shared with unfamiliar music vol.1 (guitar duets), a 2024 digital record that expanded a renewed focus on guitar as a sound source that began with releases in 2020. But what connection does this new piece have to that earlier work? The title seems to refer less to a specific genre or instrumentation and more to a mode of production, an approach to working with sound that prioritizes the strange, the dislocated, the not-quite-familiar. The cover of this release depicts Ielasi performing in Paris with a sampler, suggesting a process rooted in improvisation and constraint. And indeed, some of the samples in the piece do seem to be shared with previously released works, here recontextualized and repurposed. This is not a work of pure creation ex nihilo but of rearrangement, of finding new relationships between existing materials, a practice that echoes both the concrète tradition as well as Ielasi’s own history of pushing it into new territory. The GRM’s acousmatic tradition is evident in the microphone technique and in the spatial treatment of sounds, but there is also a digital air to the proceedings that feels distinctly contemporary, a reminder that the techniques Schaeffer pioneered have been absorbed, transformed, and rendered nearly invisible in the work of subsequent generations. Where cole and Ambarchi’s contribution moves from intimacy to surreal mundanity, Ielasi’s work operates in a different register entirely. The piece itself unfolds as a study in gentle contrast and rhythmic accumulation. The rhythmic elements that have long characterized his work are present but transformed—pulses that never quite lock into a predictable groove, small sounds that build into larger textures, a sense of propulsion that constantly threatens to derail itself. Static gives way to layers of competing rhythm gives way to a mobile lullaby. unfamiliar music (paris) passes through a range of sonic territories without any clear delineations between movements. Ielasi opts instead for a gradual process of substitution. What emerges is a piece that feels both of its moment and somehow outside of it. The “unfamiliar” of the title is not a description of the sounds themselves but of the relationships between them, the way they refuse to settle into expected patterns or resolve into comfortable listening. Ielasi makes music that demands attention without demanding understanding, that rewards close listening without promising easy rewards.   Taken together with the cole and Ambarchi piece, this release offers a portrait of the series at its best: two works that share little in common but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do, and a commitment to the kind of exploration that Schaeffer himself would have recognized. The Portraits GRM series continues to honor its institutional legacy not through preservation but through renewal, not by looking backward but by making space for the unfamiliar. (Joseph Sannicandro)

Captured during a performance at Reykjavík's Harpa Concert Hall on 24 October 2021, the show saw Björk play music mostly from 2004 album Medúlla. For the performance, she was joined by the 50-member Hamrahlíð Choir, who were conducted by Þorgerður Ingólfsdóttir. Musician Bergur Þórisson also provided accompaniment on the organ. The album will be released across vinyl, CD, DVD and Blu-ray formats, and features renditions of 11 of Björk's tracks. items.body: Eight years after Bone Bame, the Paris collective return with a record named after a Cameroonian mountain that traps walkers in a dance they cannot quit. The reason they chose that story is more pointed than the sleeve lets on Somewhere in the middle of the Bone Bame touring cycle, 10LEC6 stopped being able to work. Nicole, the singer whose voice is the entire centre of the group, was served an OQTF, the French administrative order requiring a person to leave the country. The practical result was that the band could not honour festival bookings outside France. A Paris collective built almost entirely on movement, on diaspora, on rhythms carried between continents, was pinned to one territory by paperwork. It was Nicole... items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — The debut album of the progressive rock supergroup consisting of Keith Emerson of THE NICE, Greg Lake of KING CRIMSON and Carl Palmer of ATOMIC ROOSTER. A bold statement of what was to come, with the band incorporating their classical and jazz background to their rock music.The album is a mix of original songs (Take a pebble, The three fates, Tank & Lucky man) and rock arrangements of classical music (The barbarian & Knife-edge.) Keith Emerson is the key figure of the album of course, with his bombastic playing. Carl Palmer is a really hard hitter and delivers a great drum solo as well on the track "Tank". Lake's voice is heart-warming as always, but the man can deliver some amazing bass lines as well. The album is characterized by top flight musicianship, but unfortunately not top flight songwriting, at least at some parts of it. Despite that, it is a strong album, and any album with "Take a pebble" on, is worth owning.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — If SCARLET THREAD wasn't conceived as one of those single guy projects with a revolving support system, it became one fast during the interval between their "Psykedeelisi� Joutsenlauluja" and "Valheista Kaunein", with personnel in flux right through the early recording sessions. Only JANI TIMONIEMI remained, but he did keep the guitar/violin/flute instrumental orientation, so this doesn't sound all that different from the jam-oriented and jazz accented debut. Perhaps a bit heavier in parts such as on "Jumalanilkkakirves" and "Levoton Sielu", this is still balanced with the pastoral woodwinds and strings. The opener kicks off with an irresistible riff but doesn't support it enough when offstage. Some of the numbers sound like they are just trying to get to the end, while simultaneously shrugging like they have no idea how to end it. Still, the KC trio era plus folk influences, particularly on the more succinct "Aatoksia Kivusta" and "Haarasilta" , make this a worthwhile 43 minutes, and worth returning to when the mood strikes.

The ensemble continues to present renditions of well known songs from the British Isles as well as their homeland, and once again in each case they offer a novel interpretation.Closest comparisons would be with the more politically serious MABSANT from Wales and GALAHAD from Germany, with the usual British Isles (including JETHRO TULL at their folkiest) and Breton (BERNARD BENOIT) suspects of course, and, in one track ("Lampolan Vintilla"), the as yet unformed SANGRE DE MUERDAGO. "Y� viel� on" has a go at the very first track on the very first CLANNAD album in a manner which, superior or not, fits better on this album than on that Donegal group's debut. It's a good deal more rocking with menacing fiddles. The last 2 songs respectively revisit "Tam Lin" (best known as a FAIRPORT song) and "The Twelve Witches" (STEELEYE SPAN) and to me are unrecognizable from the versions I know, with only the first somewhat signaled by its many verses. It's much more mysterious with whistles and whispered lyrics for the first part but, without following along the Finnish lyrics, I find it stays on past closing time, while I have no issues with "Twelve Witches" at all, a typically dire lyric made joyous, even in Finnish!For the rest, it's all at least good, with the best being "Hepsankaika" which introduces our character "type", the saucy fiddle-heavy "Neidon Kielto", the cello infused and at least R rated "Minulta Saisit", and the seize the day whistled exuberance of "Lampolan Vintill�".Our protagonist can succeed in seducing even the most hardened of us from track one, and isn't that her goal? She does get a lot of help from a band that is a lot more disciplined than she.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Auto Reconnaissance' is the kind of prog album you would play if you're already a fan of TheTangent (or any contemporary symphonic/retro prog band playing this kind of music), and that'sperfectly fine because every new release from the Andy Tillison-led band is a real treat. I cannotcomprehend how he has been able to come up with so many great albums, and while this particular oneis one of the most laid-back, charming, and "conventional" Tangent albums, it is still packed withsome excellent tunes and brilliant playing.The lineup here consists of drummer Steve Roberts, guitarist Luke Machine, bassist Jonas Reingold,and sax player Theo Travis, and I have the impression that this is one of the longest-lastinglineups in the history of the band, responsible for a couple of really fine records under TheTangent name.Anyway, 'Auto Reconnaissance' continues the distinctive blend of melodic retro prog and groovy jazz-rock and does not differ dramatically from its predecessors. In fact, I feel like this is one of theleast experimental albums from the group, which is nevertheless compensated for by the fineproduction and overall relaxing atmosphere of the album. Two long-form pieces appear, and in-betweenthem four standard-length tracks give us glimpses of the different musical personalities of AndyTillison. Upbeat opener 'Life on Hold' is a song I am quite keen on, probably because of its gushysynths and groove-heavy rhythm. This is followed by the nearly 16-minute-long travel log suite'Jinxed in Jersey', which is an interesting surprise and one of my favorite tracks on the album.Apart from Tillison's curious narration (of his journey in Jersey), it also covers a wide array ofstyles in a brilliant manner. The other really fun track here is 'The Tower of Babel', which is morethan I can say for the 28-minute opus 'Lie Back & Think of England'.I have listened to this piece several times and I still do not find anything exceptional or excitingabout it. It seems to be a meandering epic that explores a sequence of disparate ideas, leaving mostof them underdeveloped in the context of the whole piece. The bonus track 'Proxima' is reallyenjoyable, blending together Tillison's progressive electronic soundscapes with the jazzy playing ofhis bandmates. All in all, 'Auto Reconnaissance' by The Tangent is a really good and relaxing albumthat feels too safe to be recognized as one of their all-time best.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — And the creators of and tour guides to alternate worldscapes press on! Amazing! 1. "Guardstones" (6:40) a rambling piece that sounds more like a soundtrack piece for a documentary on Amazonian rainforests. Nice bass and drum interplay from Corey Wallace and Pat Garvey in the fourth minute. (8.75/10)2. "Space Platform" (5:57) a song that seems to have a built in reset button as it cycles around several times from spacey keyboard rhythm tracks into full-speed free-wheelin' off-road mountain biking craziness over and over again, not just once or twice but five times! Each time as the high-speed craziness melts into spacey observation mode I find myself thinking, "well, that was fun; too bad it's over" but then it returns, wave after wave. Awesome (if a bit familiar surf for the Ozrics). (9/10)3. "Harmonic Mind" (9:12) a song that actually sounds like something from THE PSYCHEDELIC ENSEMBLE: "The Golden King" from 2013's The Tale of the Golden Kings! I know this has to be purely a coincidence but the similarities are multiple and unmistakable. A little heavier with Ed's use of PETE TOWNSEND-like guitar power chords and, later, SynthAxe-like Industrial guitar sounds (think 1980s Allan Holdworth and Three of a Perfect Pair-era Robert Fripp). Eventually the guitar and keyboard work kind of trims and smooths but Pat and Corey are still flying at top speed as if they're in a real hurry to get somewhere--which makes it a challenge for the rest of the band to A) keep up and B) find inspiration. I mean, Silas continues to inject fun and interesting space-jungle sounds and riffs but Ed seems to be struggling with his guitar synthesizer, trying to find creative things to add to the mix. Interesting! (17.6667/20)4. "Malachite" (7:52) a song that seems to have trouble finding an identity. There are good intentions from Pat and Corey, but they're not finding the kind of support that one would hope for: it's as if the two front men are having trouble connecting or finding inspiration from the lines and melodies coming from the rhythm corps. Weird! There are so many instances that remind me of other artist's songs and sounds but there is just this wall preventing anything from congealing! Ed's injection of sitar and Silas' old-school TD synth sound don't work either--but Corey and Pat still seem to be having a great time; it's just too bad that all four couldn't find a connection. Still, I really enjoy just listening to Pat Garvey's enthusiastic and sublime drum play on this one. (13.125/15)5. "Tillamook" (9:11) great long interdimensional atmospheric opening (the drums and bass line don't kick in until the second half of the fourth minute!) then it's scenic highway driving, as usual, as Pat's drums and Corey's bass drive Ed to great guitar heights--but only for an abreviated time as Ed generously gives way to Silas's creative soundmaking, taking us into the forests of the Pacific Northwest and the highways that service them. A pause around 7:30 turns into another rhythm-less underwater keyboard excursion to which Ed adds some tempered and Paul Speer-like guitar riffs. Excellent song! One could not ask for more or better from Ed and the Ozrics! (18.875/20) 6. "Sumipad" (4:54) this one sounds a little traveled: as if I'm hearing a new, updated version of something they've done before (and done well, I might add). The problem is: for any Ozrics lover this is not/never a bad thing: it's great music and a great alternate reality that the band ushers us into. Such a delight! It's so hard for me to imagine someone--anyone--not loving this music! (9.333/10) Total Time 43:46Though it is always a joy to discover/uncover new Ozrics music, there is just enough of a disconnect between the rhythm section and the lead duo on this album to prevent total and satisfactory immersion within the "alternate worlds" that Ed and his crew offer us.A-/4.5 stars; a wonderful exposure to the delightful sonic worlds of Ed Wynne and his Ozric Tentacles though not quite as fully-fleshed out as one might hope. Still, "Tillamook" and "Sumipad" are not to be missed: two additions to the long list of Ozrics' "classics."

items.body: Review by meurdhek — We are dealing here with a genuine little zeuhl gem, for which Alain Lebon from Soleil Zeuhl can never be thanked enough for having rescued it from limbo, and which is bound to stir a few emotions.The listener is completely immersed in a zeuhl cauldron, with the sometimes strange yet very pleasant impression of hearing an unreleased tape from Magma's best years. The sound of Carmina, apart from a few forays into soprano saxophone and vibraphone, is very close to that of peak Magma from 1973?74.The group never repeats itself, offering ideas that are each more Magma-esque and zeuhl-driven than the last. This will undoubtedly delight fans of zeuhl music, but it also has the drawback, in my view, of slightly disorienting the listener, who may search in vain for a guiding thread within this very rich and ambitious music.One gets the impression that the band makes it a point of honor never to repeat itself and to constantly surprise the listener. Ideas come thick and fast at a sustained pace, and none is ever truly developed or explored, as the music quickly moves on to something else without any real connection between them.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Ceiba by Temic is a fantastic progressive metal album from the newest prog supergroup, showcasing great technical melodic instrumental work and great emotional vocals from Fredrik Klemp. Taking members from The Neal Morse Band, Shining, Maraton & ex Haken keyboardist Diego Tejeida, the interplay between Tejeida & Eric Gillette's melodic shredding is very impressive and at times would even give Jordan Rudess & John Petrucci a run for their money. While there are great heavy polyrhythmic moments, the focus on melody and harmony is also potent, which really gives the band an emotional edge. A spark which could be a very bright future for the project. I'd give this a mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Parting The Waves Inside.

items.body: Review by Rysiek P. — The following statement might be a bit of an exaggeration, but if one were to single out the most important Argentine - or even, I would venture to say, South American - symphonic rock band, that band would, in my opinion, be Nexus. The roots of this Argentine quintet go back to the 1970s, when a group of students from the capital, Buenos Aires, became fascinated by symphonic rock - a passion that soon led to the band's formation. However, the dream of releasing a full-length album was not realized until the late 1990s, when the group brought out its debut record, *Detr�s del Umbral*, in 1999. Their early releases are characterized by an impressive, monumental sound rich in superb keyboard parts. Powerful, expressive female vocals infuse the music with emotional depth, preventing the sense of "technical excess" or "overloading" that can sometimes plague bands relying heavily on synthesizer and organ elements in their arrangements. Their most obvious influences include the work of ELP (Hammond organ playing), Genesis's middle period (rich, symphonic sound), and Marillion (synthesizer passages). The undisputed turning point in their career was the 2001 album *Metanoia* - in my view, still one of the finest symphonic rock albums ever recorded by a South American band. Its sound is remarkably impressive, driven by rich, monumental keyboard arrangements. The album features outstanding symphonic rock compositions that captivate the listener with numerous stirring mood shifts and magnificent keyboard and guitar solos. The powerful Spanish-language vocals harmonize perfectly with the diverse atmospheres presented throughout the record. *Metanoia* embodies all the elements that make symphonic rock such a compelling genre! Among their later works, the 2011 album *La Divina Comedia*, the following year's *Aire*, and the 2023 release *Insania* all deserve attention and belong in every symphonic rock fan's collection. It is also worth checking out the recently released (2023) live album *Nexus en Concierto / Homenaje a CRUCIS* to see for yourself that the Argentinians are a great live act as well. But let's return to the main reason for this article: the latest album, *1042*, which was officially released on October 2nd of this year. Its release marks the band's 50th anniversary (their first concert took place on July 10, 1976) and features a guest appearance by Gustavo Montesano - bassist and vocalist for the group Crucis. Once again, Nexus takes the listener on a journey of over forty minutes into a realm of extraordinary sounds. Rest assured - after all, this is their tenth full-length album. Be prepared, however, to hear - right from the opening track - fundamental differences between symphonic rock in the European-American sense (which radiates a barrage of endless synthesizers and organs, often accompanied by frenetic, majestic guitar solos) and the symphonic rock of South American bands, which is bombastic yet strangely "soft" and melodic. The track "El Visitante," while serving as an instrumental intro, is also a magnificent example of this specific musical approach. It sounds powerful and assertive, yet simultaneously very melodic - almost "song-like" - with the swaying phrases of slightly subdued synthesizers. South American bands also approach the role of vocals in their music somewhat differently. This is immediately evident in the second track of the new album: "Desiertos" (Deserts) is both a magnificent composition with a perfectly chosen key and one of the release's two standout tracks. The song unfolds at a leisurely pace, and an intriguing music video - available on various platforms - illustrates its lyrical themes. This ballad-like delicacy is further enhanced by the narrative vocal style of Roxy Truccolo, a band member since 2017 (when she contributed to the album *En El Comienzo Del Topos Uranos*). Her vocals were already a superb "bonus" on the band's previous album (*Insania*), but here she sounds magnificent; she adds an element of Gothic mystery to her naturally calm timbre while steering clear of quasi-operatic tones. It is also worth noting that Roxy handles all the bass lines. The track "Sin Saber Del Sol" begins in a somewhat similar fashion. Once again, Roxy's vocals, combined with synthesizers, infuse the track - which is undeniably keyboard-driven - with an atmosphere of tranquility and a certain epic quality. Yet, this is not a composition that flaunts its synthesizer or organ sounds; rather, these elements are seamlessly woven into the musical fabric. They do not demand special attention or compel the listener to hunt for hidden sonic layers; instead, they contribute on equal footing with the vocals and rhythm section to create a composition that feels simultaneously symphonic and non-symphonic. The situation is entirely different with the track "El Otro Lado." Here, synthesizer sounds with a hard-rock edge captivate the listener through their sheer power and staccato chords. It is in this track that the "South American" sound comes closest to the "European" style, with its robust, slightly hard-rock-influenced foundation. In my opinion, the second track that makes the greatest impression on the listener is the composition "Una Ley." It is an epic piece, characterized by sweeping phrasing and melodic flourishes. It features a long instrumental introduction and piano accompaniment, against which every sung verse feels like a deeply sorrowful confession. Six minutes that reach into the deepest recesses of the musical soul. Six minutes of a truly epic musical journey in the finest symphonic style. The final track - "Periplo Del Ego" - showcases the band's improvisational prowess. Naturally, this display unfolds against a backdrop of flawless musical backing. There are Emerson-esque keyboards, powerful drum hits, and a structure entirely driven by the instruments. It is nearly twelve minutes of sheer mastery, allowing each musician to showcase their skills in a way that creates a multidimensional composition - a brilliant example of modern symphonic rock. On the version of the album I own, the band serves up "Teaser Album 1042 - Bonus Track" right at the end - a preview of the record's musical content that had previously appeared here and there as promotional material. It's the album in a nutshell: three minutes containing a bit of everything. Just a nice little extra for the fans. In summary? The album *1042* restores faith in symphonic rock while reminding us that, alongside the familiar varieties, there exists another - the South American kind. It is distinctive, unlike the versions we usually encounter: mellow, song-oriented, lyrical, and epic. A great deal is happening - or is about to happen - in the world of symphonic rock this year. We have already seen a release from The Neal Morse Band, with new albums from The Flower Kings and Neal Morse & The Resonance arriving shortly. The latest offerings from Khatsaturjan and The Samurai of Prog have also shone brightly on the musical horizon. We have only just listened to the new double album from Andy Tillison's The Tangent. It will be difficult to pick a single "best" album this year. That is why I increasingly feel the need to create two separate lists: one for "progressive" albums and another for "unconventional crossover" releases - a move I feel somewhat compelled to make as a "musical Darwinist." This time, it simply won't all fit into one category... (sic!). Published also at MLWZ.pl

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. Intro (Mafar) featuring local vocals, a melancholic guitar sound worthy of Anathema, a melody reminiscent of the *The Persuaders!* theme, and stereo keyboards undulating between the speakers. Elegance, abstract Oriental rock, traditional instruments?in short, a perfect soundscape evoking life in a land that symbolizes religious massacres.2. "Nsina El 'Inwan" follows?a sad, intimate ballad driven by piano and a resigned-sounding guitar; Jeries' vocals demonstrate how a voice, when well-integrated into a tune, enhances the track without stifling the melody.3. "Min El Nar Khayfen" features crystalline keyboard work answering a sparkling guitar, with a touch of vintage organ. Philippe launches a killer guitar solo?a moment suggesting that peace is actually possible.4. "Esma' O Shouf" shifts into new-wave/darkwave mode; the rhythm guitar starts with a 60s "gangster" vibe before drifting into an 80s Marillion style, then moving toward the new-millennium sound of Riverside?fabulous. And let's not forget Raji's organ, which melts the heart; in short, it's great to rediscover them and dive back into their music.5. "Fatah 'Eneih" follows, built on a plaintive organ and guitar interplay. It has a sluggish start, then builds into a crescendo of incredible tension that wanders off into dreamlike prog, flirting with black/heavy/prog metal. Marwan's bass rides a Pink Floyd wave before washing up against a jazzy piano; the prog sound drifts along with an austere heavy riff and a haunting, persistent keyboard line. Never a dull moment.6. "Ana Malet" features a groovy, grunge-tinged riff and vocals worthy of the Sex Pistols?throwing caution to the wind: where are they headed? In any case, it's delightful to see this fusion of styles. Just as I'm settling in, the thunderous 80s-style sax from Jeries pulls us back into mainstream rock. A touch of melancholic guitar?reminiscent of Anathema?and I'm hooked.7. "El Leil Bhal 'Oyoun" returns to the Mafar sound?a welcome shift. It's a bouncy alternative track, driven by distant, heavy guitar notes. A flirtation between metal and dark rock, with the sax magically tying it all together. A track that shines thanks to its build-up and that melancholic guitar?it's a real thrill for me?leading into a soaring finale that veers into metal for that massive sound.8. "Sada" follows, pulling the same trick: a restrained, metallic guitar riff punching through against a backdrop of ethereal piano. The Anathema vibe keeps coming back to me; the piano outro, gently picking out its final notes, is simply admirable.9. The true "Outro" arrives, blending synth, violin, and melancholic guitar, all bolstered by a rich, melting organ?pure listening pleasure.An album to help you live?almost as if nothing were wrong?in this dehumanized territory; a little music to help you survive.

items.body: Review by Matti — The focus wasn't very sharp yet, when the newly formed Amsterdam-based quartet went to London to record their debut album in January 1970. At the time they had secured a five-month slot at the Amsterdam cast of the hippie musical Hair. Of course the musicians, namely guitarist Jan Akkerman and Thijs van Leer (organ, piano, vocals), with a rhythm section that was to be replaced for the next album, already had several years' experience in rock music, separately. If this album (and the band) was a one-off case instead of being a prelude to the all-time greatest chapter of Dutch prog, undoubtedly it would be at least a "hidden prog gem" or maybe even an established early classic. But Focus was to reach so much higher levels that if the already charmed listener at some point enters their debut, it won't be an ubforgettable affair. Three stars is the best I can give.Focus at their prime (and ever since) were very much an instrumental act, so the large amount of vocal pieces is the most interesting feature here. The nearly 10-minute opener 'Focus' is, however, an instrumental and surely shows the way the band was heading at, but I can't help feeling it simply loses its focus and feels over-extended,despite containing beautiful melodies. Akkerman's electric guitar solo lacks elegance and goes on too long. 'Why Dream' is a 4-minute ballad-ish song sung by Thijs with bassist Martijn Dresden's backing vocals. Slightly reminiscent of the obscure, late 60's Pink Floyd songs sung by Rick Wright, except that the electric guitar dominates the latter half.The drug dealing lyrics for 'Happy Nightmare (Mescaline)' were written by Mike Hayes for Dresden particularily. This rather peaceful song has a nice jazzy flair, and the guitar solo, unlike on the previous track, is thankfully followed by a brief return to the song substance. The dynamic 7-minute instrumental 'Anonymus' suffers from the similar blurred focus and the taste of unnecessary extension as 'Focus'. The Focus trademarks, even a hint of Old Music, are there, but in a jam-like form to show off the group's technical competence, especially speaking of their most recent member Akkerman whose classically influenced composing skills are only carefully starting to bloom on this album.'Black Beauty' is an OK melodic song that - without the irritatingly sharp-sounding guitar - would pass as a mediocre Moody Blues song c. 1968. 'Sugar Island' is a merry song about Cuba with silly lyrics. No wonder it was omitted from the album's US edition. The serene closing piece 'Focus (Vocal)' is a little revisitation to a theme heard on the opener, featuring calm and terribly brief vocals, but somehow even it, in less than 3 minutes, loses the focus and just continues the simple musical phrase. Pretty but boring.The lively, Jethro Tull reminding flute-heavy instrumental 'House of King' was wisely added to the album's later editions. It has the sharp rhythm a bit too much on the surface, but otherwise it's charming in its simplicity. All in all, this debut has no ghost of a chance competing with the real Focus classics.

items.body: Review by meurdhek — Nearly 50 years that we've been waiting for these recordings! They have finally reached us in the form of a CD packed to the brim.Here, then, is Xalph, with its creative and warm take on Zeuhl, embracing us and happily plunging us back into the excitement of those years at the end of Magma's first incarnation, when excellent bands emerged from its orbit and carved their own paths through the lava of the world Magma had created.Besides shedding some Soleil Zeuhl light on these recordings, this edition finally sets the record straight, putting things back in order and into perspective, after the Monster M�lodies edition made two mistakes when the LP was released in 2018.The first stated: "This record contains the track 'Gya-Tei' in its entirety, a track of which only part had previously appeared on the Enneade compilation of new music, released in 1987."Yet this track had in fact already been released in its entirety on the Enneade compilation...The second claim was made with no small amount of audacity, or perhaps simply out of ignorance: "This record contains all of this legendary group's studio recordings."We now know that this was false. In fact, all the recordings on this CD had already been circulating online for decades under the title "Demos 1975-1980", albeit in inferior-sounding versions.One could even argue that the best tracks were not chosen for the Monster M�lodies LP. "Xessanderelph", "Exorde" and "Ter" keep you on the edge of your seat, and while some of the other tracks may initially seem softer, with occasional lulls, every track contains passages and endings of epic, exultant, even blazing progressive Zeuhl. This is further reinforced by the addition of vocals, which undoubtedly immerse Xalph even more deeply in the genre's established conventions, shaped by the model that bears Vander's signature, while pushing the jazz-rock aspect of their music slightly further into the background.With the exception of Gya-Tei, all the tracks presented here had therefore remained unreleased in this particular form. Nevertheless, we find the intro to "Entr�e d'Am�lie" and "Ballade � Xalph" on the LP in earlier versions that one might even prefer. The addition of soprano saxophone undoubtedly gives them a more soaring lyrical quality, while the later versions recorded at Studio Isis bring a more pronounced sense of tension, with the guitar pushed further to the forefront.In any case, if I were to indulge in a shortcut, I would say that Xessander's presents countless moments of musical grace and daring, drawn from the finest vintage of Zeuhl jazz-rock lava. It would have been a shame if we had never had the chance to enjoy them.

items.body: Review by Logan — The history of Boc Maxima functions like a rogue transmission. Distributed as a private 1996 cassette to a small inner circle of family and friends, it eventually leaked into the early-2000s file-sharing ether and became a foundational internet myth. Rather than a mere collection of loose bedroom demos, the tape serves as the unredacted genetic blueprint for what Boards of Canada would become. Context alters the architecture. A sound wave does not change its geometry, but its impact shifts based on the reified bounds of the sequence. Sequenced between dark, lo-fi vignettes and deliberate, haunting fade-ins, these familiar melodies lose their polished studio insulation. The timeline functions less like a passive playlist and more like a continuous midnight broadcast.The movement of this tape carries the uncanny dimensions of The Twilight Zone, where science meets superstition, alongside the OBLIVION signal in Cronenberg's Videodrome, and the unrepeatable frequency of the 1977 Wow! signal. The bleeding transitions carry a distinct Blue Jam late-night radio logic. The sequencing introduces an invasive quality that alters how the listening space decodes this familiar pastoral nostalgia, inducing a state of quiet suspension where childhood memory and cold, apocalyptic dread exist in an uneasy harmony. Long live the new flesh.

On 2 October it came back in two remixes on UK-based digital dub and reggae label Superchip: raggamuffin boom-bap from Hopebullet, a DJ and sound engineer from Osaka who also goes by Ranking Jin, and a second version by RJD. Behind it are deejay Daddy Cookiz and producer Simma, with singer Ponchita Peligros as guest. Simma is Nathan Simm from Hull, England, a producer and DJ who started out in Ableton during the 2020 lockdown, runs Superchip and also records as Polyecho and Square Nath. His 2024 debut, Simma Enters The Game, mixed digital reggae, dubbed-out hip-hop and 8-bit chiptune and drew on the German label Jahtari and the Scottish sound system Mungo’s Hi Fi. Daddy Cookiz has deejayed since 2005 and grew up on Jamaican sound system culture, and he takes his cues from Super Cat, Yellowman and Shabba Ranks. On the album he deejays in that rub-a-dub tradition over Simma’s digital sound, and Simma now takes that sound to Japan, where he performs with Hopebullet in Kyoto on 10 October, Tokyo on 19 October and Yokohama on 21 October, in a showcase for Superchip. items.body: New York-based musician Edley ODowd, formerly of Psychic TV, will release his second solo album, “Kowai-Yet,” on November 26, 2026 via the French label Arsenic Solaris. The ambient and experimental record follows his 2022 debut, “F(our)-Ward,” and arrives on vinyl and digital, with the Pink LP edition limited to 200 copies. ODowd recorded “Kowai-Yet” over three years in multiple locations. The album brings together material he made with collaborators he has worked with since leaving New York City to live closer to nature five years ago. The seven-track record shifts from the sound-collage approach of “F(our)-Ward” toward a more emotional register. “Where F(our)-Ward was more about sound collage, Kowai-Yet is about emotion,” ODowd says. “It’s infused with joy as well as a heaping dose of sadness.” The album’s title traces back to a single word. Describing a drive home on a summer night, ODowd recalls the sound of crickets against his car tires on humid pavement as both “sinister but compelling.” The Japanese word “kowai,” meaning “scary,” came to him first. At a stop sign, as the air went still, “quiet” followed, and the two merged into “Kowai-yet.” Individual tracks trace separate origins. “Heat” took shape through an improvised studio session in Los Angeles with engineer Joo Joo Ashworth, built from a drum pattern and expanded with analog electronics set against ODowd’s backwards saxophone. “Again” began as a more traditional song ODowd wrote alone. British musician Gore Tech later added a sharper beat, two guitarists contributed parts, and singer Zoah, whom ODowd met at a coffee shop along the Delaware River, added vocals and lyrics. “Arbiter” reworks stems ODowd had originally recorded for an unfinished song about his friend Lady Jaye Breyer P-Orridge. Its choruses use samples recorded during a 2000 trip to Nepal with Lady Jaye and Genesis P-Orridge, manipulated into the track. His Problem Addict collaborator Andrew Mann closes the song with guitar feedback. “Kowai-Yet” tracklist: 1. “Jamesey” 2. “Arbiter” 3. “Again” 4. “(Bruce Was) Kicked Out Of The Band” 5. “Heat” 6. “Sunrise” 7. “You’ll Never Know” Kowai-Yet release details “Kowai-Yet” is out November 26, 2026 via Arsenic Solaris as a digital album and a Pink LP limited to 200 copies. Both are available to pre-order on Bandcamp, where the track “Heat” is streaming now. Photo credits: Trevor Gregory. Kowai-Yet by Edley ODowd About Edley ODowd Edley ODowd grew up in the suburbs outside New York City and moved to Manhattan in the late 1980s, shortly after finishing high school. He got his start on a secondhand drum kit his mother bought him at a garage sale when he was 13. During a semester abroad in London in 1991, he joined the shoegaze band The Butterflies. Back in New York, he played drums and DJed for Toilet Boys, a band that wound down after a major European tour supporting the Red Hot Chili Peppers. In 2003, ODowd was instrumental in reviving Psychic TV, persuading Genesis P-Orridge to perform again. The reunited band’s first show took place at The Coral Room in New York City on December 5, 2003. ODowd founded the label Angry Love Productions after a self-funded Psychic TV EP sold out its 230 copies within two weeks. The “PTV3” lineup of Psychic TV played its final show on November 15, 2018. Alongside music, ODowd has worked as a graphic designer for major labels since 1993, taught courses at several universities in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and worked as a mental health counselor, including as a front-line worker during the COVID-19 pandemic. ODowd released his debut solo album, “F(our)-Ward,” as a self-released, ultra-limited cassette via Flesh Prison/DeathBed Tapes in 2022. Side-Line covered its expanded reissue, “F(our) ward,” released as a trifold-sleeved CD with three bonus tracks via the Italian label 13 on February 23, 2023. That same year, ODowd formed the death rock band Scorpion Tea with Christian Cruz, singer Anthony Diaz and bassist Fern Puma, signing to the label GIVE/TAKE. Side-Line covered the band’s debut single, “Scarlet Misquote,” in June 2023, ahead of the band’s self-titled debut album. ODowd now lives about an hour’s drive from New York City, where he continues to split his time between graphic design clients, band rehearsals and recording. “Kowai-Yet,” his second solo album, is set for release on November 26, 2026 via Arsenic Solaris.

items.body: Israeli gothic metal band Fatum Aeternum has rebuilt “P.W.Y.P.” for a streaming release, bringing the track back from their 2012 EP “The Sermon.” The self-released single went out digitally on 25 September 2026. The new version keeps the original ’80s glam-rooted guitar riff while adding aggressive male vocals, a female counter voice, cello and a full gospel choir. Where the 2012 recording leaned on social commentary, the rebuilt arrangement expands it into a more layered, theatrical gothic sound the band describes as a dark sermon. “P.W.Y.P.” is the second single in Fatum Aeternum’s renewed run of releases, following the comeback single “As Above, So Below” on 25 August 2026. That single introduced a new six-piece lineup – Steve Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant – which also plays on “P.W.Y.P.” The track was recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK. Denis Saenko handled mixing and mastering, with additional mixing by Gershin; Tayo Olawepo arranged and recorded the choir. The band’s promotional materials cite Lacrimosa, Therion and Haggard as reference points. “P.W.Y.P.” is available to stream on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Amazon Music, Deezer and SoundCloud. About Fatum Aeternum Fatum Aeternum formed in Tel Aviv, Israel, in 2006, built around Steve Gershin on mandolin, bass and vocals, alongside Ze’ev Gut on fiddle and vocals and Olga Braverman on flute and vocals. The group’s first full lineup added Ilya Surnin on drums, Dan Yoffe on guitar and Rivka Aizenberg on viola, playing a self-described “renaissance metal” blend of folk and metal. Braverman left in 2007 and Gut in 2008, staying on as a guest musician as the band shifted toward a heavier, more electrified sound. Gershin considered disbanding the group in 2009 and recorded a memorial album of earlier material instead; Evelyn Shor Gershin joined permanently around the same time, stabilising the lineup. The band re-recorded its debut album “This Dream Is Dead” several times before releasing it on CD in 2011. On 24 September 2011, Fatum Aeternum played the 12th Children of the Night Gothic Festival in Kyiv, Ukraine, its first show outside Israel, sharing the bill with Waves Under Water and Diary of Dreams. The video for “Apocalypse Now” followed on YouTube in April 2012 and aired on MTV Israel’s “Headbangers Ball” that June. The band self-released the EP “The Sermon” in September 2012, recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK, and opened for Apoptygma Berzerk the same month before going on hiatus in 2013. Gershin and Evelyn Shor Gershin rebuilt the lineup with George Falk and Igor May in 2014, releasing the single “One Bastard” that April and the maxi-single “The Pain” later the same year. The EP “The Darkest Hour” followed in 2015, then “Mass Suicide of Human Race” in 2017 and “Singing Songs of Desperation” in 2020. Fatum Aeternum returned in 2026 after a three-year gap, a pause the band’s own site attributes to health issues within the group. The comeback single “As Above, So Below” arrived on 25 August 2026 with a new six-piece lineup of Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant. “P.W.Y.P.,” a rebuilt version of the 2012 “The Sermon” track, follows as the second single in that renewed run.

items.body: David J, a co-founder, bassist and co-songwriter of the post-punk bands Bauhaus and Love and Rockets, releases the single “Requiem for the Rose Garden” on 51 Recordings on 8 October 2026. The song is a protest aimed at the Trump administration, built around the White House Rose Garden as a target that is both symbolic and literal. It is the first track confirmed from J’s new album “Postcards from the Afterlife,” due 27 November on double LP, CD and digital formats. David J on ‘Requiem for the Rose Garden’ J points to physical changes made at the White House since Donald Trump’s first term in office when he explains the song. “It’s basically a protest about Trump’s administration and the atrocities it has visited upon the USA,” he said. “In the context of the song, the Rose Garden at the White House can be seen as a symbolic metaphor, although it is also quite literal. I actually wrote it during Trump’s first term in office when he had that beautiful garden hacked up. Now, even more horror has been inflicted on it of course, and the elegant East Wing of the building completely decimated which is also highly symbolic.” The backing band on the track is Duende, a Detroit-based group J has worked with extensively in the past. “Requiem for the Rose Garden” streams on Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal, Deezer and Pandora via davidjhaskins.com. ‘Postcards from the Afterlife’ due in November on 51 Recordings “Postcards from the Afterlife” is a 14-song album featuring a revolving cast of musicians and numerous autobiographical references. J sums up its themes as circling the same idea from several angles: “essentially about the poignant persistence of connection, be it in life or in death. Schisms and transitions. Love found and love lost. Requiems, reflection and revelation.” Several tracks carry string arrangements, including a finale recorded with members of the Prague Symphony and Philharmonic Orchestras. The rest of the album moves between soulful material, hazy 1960s orchestral pop, European-style chanson and the alternative rock territory J is best known for. “Postcards from the Afterlife” is released on double LP, CD and digital on 27 November. Tour dates for David J David J tours the UK through December 2026, with additional shows in Portugal, Germany and Greece around the “Postcards from the Afterlife” release. 27 November – Porto, Portugal 28 November – Lisbon, Portugal 1 December – London, UK – Moth Club 2 December – Reading, UK – Face Bar 4 December – Hebden Bridge, UK – Trades Club 5 December – Liverpool, UK – Rough Trade 8 December – Edinburgh, UK – The Voodoo Rooms 9 December – Glasgow, UK – Stereo 10 December – Newcastle, UK – The Cluny 11 December – Birmingham, UK – Hare & Hounds 13 December – Brighton, UK – Daltons 15 December – Athens, Greece – Death Disco 17 December – Berlin, Germany – Frannz Club About David J David J, born David John Haskins on 24 April 1957 in Northampton, England, co-founded Bauhaus in 1978, playing bass and co-writing songs including the group’s debut single, “Bela Lugosi’s Dead.” He sang lead vocals on “Who Killed Mr Moonlight?” Bauhaus split in 1983 and has reformed periodically since. Before Love and Rockets, J spent two years as bassist and co-producer for The Jazz Butcher, led by Pat Fish, working on the albums “A Scandal in Bohemia” (1984) and “Sex and Travel” (1985). He formed Love and Rockets in 1985 with fellow former Bauhaus members Daniel Ash and his younger brother Kevin Haskins, playing bass and sharing vocals and songwriting across seven albums released between 1985 and 1998. Both bands have reformed at intervals since their original breakups. J maintained a solo career alongside both bands. He released “Etiquette of Violence” in 1983, “Crocodile Tears and the Velvet Cosh” in 1985 and the singles compilation “On Glass” in 1986. His 1990 album “Songs from Another Season” produced the single “I’ll Be Your Chauffeur,” which reached number one on the Modern Rock Tracks chart. “Urban Urbane” followed in 1992, then “Estranged” in 2003, “Not Long for This World” in 2011 and “An Eclipse of Ships” in 2014. His memoir, “Who Killed Mister Moonlight? (Bauhaus, Black Magick and Benediction),” was published by Jawbone Press in 2014. In 2019 J released the double LP “Missive to an Angel From the Halls of Infamy and Allure.” Side-Line covered the album’s single “I Only Hear Silence Now,” featuring Emily Jane White, alongside a run of 2020 tour dates that included Bauhaus shows at Primavera Sound and Release Athens Festival. “What The Patrons Heard,” a ten-track set of originals and covers recorded over 34 years and first issued to Patreon subscribers, followed on CD and digital on 25 March 2022, with a limited numbered vinyl edition. J’s triple album of archival demos, “Tracks from the Attic,” was announced in February 2024 and released that year. He self-released the spoken-word album “The Mother Tree,” recorded with the band RAQIA, on 6 June 2025. He returned to the “Tracks from the Attic” material in March 2026 with a companion album, “Tracks From the Attic Revisited,” which Side-Line discussed with him the following month in the interview “David J Opens the Attic.” This month’s single and the album that follows continue that run of archival and new recordings.

items.body: English musician Bruce Gilbert, a founding member of Wire, plays a solo live set at Café OTO in London on Friday 9 October 2026. The night is billed as “The Hotel presents…” and also features Rocheman and performance artist Finn Kennedy. Doors are at 7:30pm, with tickets priced from £13 for Café OTO members up to £20 on the door, available through the venue. The show is The Hotel’s third evening at Café OTO in 2026. Gilbert’s set previews a new album due from The Hotel later this year. Test pressings of the as-yet-unannounced record will be sold at the merch table. Finn Kennedy premieres a newly commissioned piece titled “Streams.” Rocheman closes the night with a full band set, performing as a quartet with Fred Lomas on lead guitar, Tom Powell on drums and Tom Wright on keyboards. Rocheman’s second album, “Basin,” was released on vinyl by The Hotel earlier in 2026, following the EPs “Angel Storm” and “Virtua Saint” on Mindseyerecords.xyz. The self-directed feature film “Taurus,” due in 2027, is among the artist’s forthcoming work. Tickets for The Hotel at Café OTO Tickets cost £13 for Café OTO members, £17 in advance and £20 on the door, available through the venue’s event page. About Bruce Gilbert Bruce Gilbert, born Bruce Clifford Gilbert on 18 May 1946 in Watford, England, co-founded Wire in London in 1976 alongside Colin Newman, Graham Lewis and Robert Gotobed, playing guitar in the band until he left in 2004, following the release of the album “Send.” After Wire’s first breakup in 1980, Gilbert formed a series of projects with bassist Graham Lewis, including Cupol, Dome, P’o and Duet Emmo. Side-Line covered the 2022 remastered reissue of Duet Emmo’s sole album, “Or So It Seems,” Gilbert’s trio recording with Lewis and Daniel Miller. Gilbert also worked with A.C. Marias, producing the single “Drop/So” in 1980 for the group’s Dome label and co-producing the 1989 album “One of Our Girls (Has Gone Missing),” sharing songwriting credit with Angela Conway. Gilbert’s solo albums include “This Way” (1984), “The Shivering Man” (1987) and “Ab Ovo” (1996), all released on Mute, followed by “Ordier” (2004), “Oblivio Agitatum” (2009, Editions Mego) and “Diluvial” (2013, Touch), a collaboration with BAW. He also performs as a DJ under the name DJ Beekeeper. Wire continued without Gilbert after his departure, releasing the mini-album “Nocturnal Koreans” in 2016. Gilbert now appears at Café OTO as part of The Hotel’s third London show of 2026, ahead of a new album the label is set to release later this year.

items.body: German-Finnish futurepop duo PLATRONiC will release the three-track EP “The Emperor’s New Clothes” on 16 October 2026, with three new takes on their March single “Fortress of Fools.” The song started with a poem written by Kay Burden, inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Emperor’s New Clothes.” Kay originally had a storytelling ballad in mind. Then Sami Jumppanen presented her with a considerably more danceable instrumental, and “Fortress of Fools” became something else entirely. PLATRONiC build three new versions of ‘Fortress of Fools’ For the new EP, they have gone back to the song and, appropriately enough, given it three new “dresses.” The first, “The Dark Electro Country Dress,” is a collaboration with On Moral Ends, the Linköping-based electronic project of Swedish songwriter, singer and multi-instrumentalist Andreas Svensson. His work moves through different electronic and alternative styles, making the collaboration a rather unusual match for PLATRONiC’s futurepop side. For “The Synthpop Mashup Dress,” PLATRONiC worked with Finnish keyboardist, producer and remixer Imppu from Lahti. His work stretches from danceable synthpop to more cinematic electronic sounds, and he has also created remixes and reworks for former Kraftwerk member Wolfgang Flür. The third version stays with Kay and Sami themselves: “The Dark Medieval Gothic Dress.” According to PLATRONiC, “Fortress of Fools” spent several weeks in the Top 10 of both the Klangwald Charts and GEWC following its release earlier this year. The track reached #8 in the Klangwald Charts. The video for “Fortress of Fools” was filmed in Savonlinna, Finland, and Alicante, Spain, and was created and produced by PLATRONiC. PLATRONiC formed in 2020 and consists of German singer-songwriter and co-producer Kay Burden and Finnish composer and producer Sami Jumppanen. Side-Line readers may also know the duo from “How To Ride The Wave,” which appeared earlier this year on Side-Line’s The Freya Files Ukraine benefit compilation. “The Emperor’s New Clothes” tracklist: 1. “Fortress of Fools – The Dark Electro Country Dress” (PLATRONiC & On Moral Ends) 2. “Fortress of Fools – The Synthpop Mashup Dress” (PLATRONiC & Imppu) 3. “Fortress of Fools – The Dark Medieval Gothic Dress” (PLATRONiC) Before the three new “dresses” arrive, “Fortress of Fools” already has its own visual counterpart. “The Emperor’s New Clothes” is available to pre-save via DistroKid ahead of its 16 October release. About PLATRONiC PLATRONiC released the single “Now!” in June 2022, followed by the EP “The Healing” in April 2023 and a cover of Depeche Mode’s “The Things You Said” that August. A reworked version of their debut single “Pride” followed in June 2024, then the winter single “Winter Stores” that December. In March 2025, they released the teaser video for “How to Ride the Wave,” and in December 2025 contributed a cover of Depeche Mode’s “But Not Tonight” to the “In Your Memory 2” tribute compilation. “Fortress of Fools” followed in March 2026 as the duo’s most recent original single, ahead of “The Emperor’s New Clothes” EP arriving on 16 October.

items.body: Cleopatra Records will issue “Drink the New Wine”, the last studio recording by post-punk and goth rock band Bauhaus, as a 12-inch vinyl single on 30 October 2026. The pressing comes in three hand-numbered, etched color variants – white, silver and red – capped at 150 copies each, for a total of 450. Peter Murphy, Daniel Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins recorded the track separately during COVID-19 lockdown. The four traded audio files using the surrealist “exquisite corpse” method the band had used before. Bauhaus released it digitally in March 2022, its first new song since the 2008 album “Go Away White.” No Bauhaus recording has followed. Ash confirmed in April 2023 that the band’s reunion had ended, with the surviving members reforming Love and Rockets. ‘Drink the New Wine’: a lockdown recording now on hand-numbered vinyl Ash describes the track as typical of the band’s more playful side. “I always loved it when Bauhaus would go into art fart mode. Truly liberating and FUN!” he said. Cleopatra Records calls the release “a music artifact […] created for the most dedicated Bauhaus fans and collectors.” Side A of the single holds “Drink the New Wine.” Side B is etched with a reproduction of the Bauhaus logo and carries no audio. Each copy is individually hand-numbered, one color per customer, with no repressing planned once the 450 copies sell out. The single is available for pre-order through Cleopatra Records ahead of the 30 October release. About Bauhaus Small Wonder Records released Bauhaus’s debut single, “Bela Lugosi’s Dead,” in August 1979, a year after Peter Murphy, Daniel Ash, David J (David John Haskins) and his younger brother Kevin Haskins formed the band in Northampton, England. The single arrived before goth existed as a named scene. Four studio albums followed in four years on 4AD and Beggars Banquet: “In the Flat Field” (1980), “Mask” (1981), “The Sky’s Gone Out” (1982) and “Burning from the Inside” (1983). Bauhaus split on 5 July 1983, a week before “Burning from the Inside” reached shops. The pioneering band reunited for a 1998 tour and again from 2005 to 2008, a run that produced a fifth album, “Go Away White” (2008, Cooking Vinyl), released without a supporting tour. Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins had already carried their partnership into Love and Rockets, formed in 1985, and into separate solo careers. David J’s catalog includes the albums “Etiquette of Violence” and “Songs from Another Season,” plus a 2014 memoir, “Who Killed Mister Moonlight?” The four original members reunited again in 2019, announcing Peter Murphy’s first live date with Bauhaus after a heart attack ahead of shows at the Hollywood Palladium that November. A further reunion tour followed in 2022, covering Europe and the US West Coast. Months after the band released “Drink the New Wine,” Murphy’s rehab admission forced it to cancel the rest of its North American tour that August. Ash ended the reunion in April 2023, and the surviving trio returned to Love and Rockets. David J has stayed active since. He revisited his own archive on the album ‘Tracks From the Attic Revisited’ and discussed the project earlier this year in a Side-Line interview. This is the first time “Drink the New Wine” has been pressed to a physical format.

items.body: Finnish electropunk duo I Think I Broke Something releases the single “Decadence” on 7 October 2026. The track is the third single from the duo’s upcoming EP “Another Escape,” due November 5, and the release will be marked with a show at Semifinal in Helsinki the same day. The band calls “Decadence” one of its most accessible tracks to date: “In our world, Decadence is a fairly straightforward electro-industrial punk track. You could describe it as a collision between Viagra Boys and The Prodigy, while still doing its own weird thing in its own universe. It’s probably one of the most radio-friendly tracks we’ve ever made.” Decadence by I Think I Broke Something “Decadence” follows “Illegal,” released August 6, and “Heads Up,” released September 9, as the third single from “Another Escape” ahead of the EP’s November 5 release. “Decadence” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp and Spotify. About I Think I Broke Something I Think I Broke Something, also known as ITIBS, is a Helsinki-based duo made up of Jouni and Miika, active since 2014. The project debuted with the EP “Superman Sabotage Clan” and has since released three full-length albums, including “Still Not Going To,” announced for an October 26, 2022 release as the duo’s third LP, alongside numerous singles and remixes through various labels. That album cycle included the singles “Astral,” released September 2022, “Corpse,” released April 2023, and “Raw,” released July 2023. ITIBS describes its sound as a distorted electronic hybrid that draws on The Prodigy, 3TEETH and Nine Inch Nails and mixes explosive electronics with metal-heavy weight. The duo lists collaborations with The Prodigy’s Maxim, DJ Hyper and Zardonic. “Decadence,” released October 7, follows “Illegal” and “Heads Up” as the third single from the EP “Another Escape,” due November 5 alongside the band’s release show at Semifinal in Helsinki.

items.body: Town & Towers Records releases Purwien & Kowa‘s new single “Italo-disco in San Francisco” on 9 October 2026, ahead of the German synth-pop duo’s sixth studio album, “Sechs,” due 23 October on the same label. The digital single carries four tracks: German and English versions of “Italo-disco in San Francisco,” an extended “Irgendwas ist immer (12″ Mix)” and a combined “German English Mashup 12″ mix” of the title track. Both language versions of the lyrics string together a run of 1980s references, naming figures including Lady Diana, Mikhail Gorbachev, Blondie, Phil Collins, Falco and Michael Jackson alongside songs such as “Blue Monday,” “Tainted Love,” “Like a Virgin,” “Take On Me,” “99 Luftballons,” “Forever Young” and “The Final Countdown.” “Italo-disco in San Francisco” mixes Italo disco, synthpop, New Wave and EBM, and follows the singles “Concorde” and “Hinter Glas” as the third preview of “Sechs.” Italo-disco in San Francisco by Purwien & Kowa About Purwien & Kowa Purwien & Kowa is a German synth-pop duo based in Dortmund formed by Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa. Purwien co-founded the electronic/darkwave act Second Decay in 1987, initially under the name Blue Velvet, together with Andreas Michael Sippel. Second Decay released the tape “Monochromes” in 1988 and the 12-inch “Killing Desire” in 1989, followed by “La Décadence Électronique” on CD in 1992, the “Hinter Glas” maxi-CD in 1993 and the album “Taste” in 1994. The band continued with “Der Nerv” in 1995, “Familiar” in 1997, “The Hunt” and “De Luxe” in 1998, “Hotels” in 1999 and “Kaltes, weißes Licht” in 2001, before pausing new material after the 2002 live release “Zwischenfall 1999.” Thomas Kowa, born Thomas Kowalzik in 1969 in Ludwigshafen am Rhein, joined the German synth-pop band No Comment in 1989 and has lived in Switzerland since 2007. He founded the label Nanopop in 2001, closing it in 2007 to focus on writing. Since 2012 he has published a series of crime novels and thrillers. His other current music projects include Nine Seconds and Emily Kinski’s dead. Purwien and Kowa began recording together as Purwien & Kowa, releasing the three-EP digital set “Drei” via Zwei Records in October 2018. The duo also co-hosts the Disko 80 podcast, which covers 1980s music and has featured more than 100 episodes with guests including Joachim Witt, Bernhard Lloyd of Alphaville and Marcus Meyn of Camouflage. Kowa separately co-hosts the “Krimi Schweiz” podcast on Swiss crime fiction. Purwien and Kowa also record together as Heldautomat, whose own single “Liebe ist endlich” reached Town & Towers Records on the same day as “Italo-disco in San Francisco.” The duo performed at the 18th Elektrisch Festival in 2026. Purwien & Kowa returned this year with the singles “Concorde,” “Hinter Glas” and “Italo-disco in San Francisco,” ahead of their sixth studio album, “Sechs,” produced by Olaf Wollschläger and due 23 October 2026 via Town & Towers Records.

items.body: Town & Towers Records releases Heldautomat‘s new single “Liebe ist endlich” on October 9, 2026. It is the third single from the Dortmund, Germany duo’s debut album “Zwischen den Lichtern”, due October 23 on the same label. “Liebe ist endlich” (“Love is finite”) opens with a slow synthesizer introduction before settling into a synth-pop arrangement, with Christian Purwien’s vocals staying restrained throughout. The refrain states its theme directly: “Liebe ist endlich / Sie ist leider vergänglich” (“Love is finite / Unfortunately, it is transient”). Heldautomat describe the track on Bandcamp as a song with “no metaphors, no way out, no redemption. Just the quiet realisation that things come to an end.” Purwien writes the lyrics and sings. Kowa plays the synthesizers. Olaf Wollschläger produced the single. Club mix and video for ‘Liebe ist endlich’ The digital release also includes a “Videomix” of the duo’s first single, “Am ersten Tag”, and a club mix of “Liebe ist endlich” produced by Purwien & Kowa, Purwien and Kowa’s other recording project. Heldautomat also posted an official video for “Liebe ist endlich” on YouTube. “Liebe ist endlich” is open for digital pre-order on Bandcamp. Liebe ist endlich by Heldautomat About Heldautomat Heldautomat is the Dortmund, Germany duo of Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa, working with analogue synthesizers, piano and a drum machine alongside Purwien’s vocals. Purwien co-founded Second Decay in Witten in 1987 with Andreas Michael Sippel, after the pair had performed as Blue Velvet from 1985. Second Decay recorded entirely on analogue synthesizers and released albums including “Taste” (1994) and “The Hunt” (1998) before going quiet after 2002. Emmo.Biz Records has since reissued “The Hunt” on green double vinyl and “Taste” on a second double-LP edition. Purwien and Kowa also record together as Purwien & Kowa, a project with five albums behind it and a sixth, “Sechs”, in the works. The duo played the 18th Elektrisch Festival on February 27, 2026, in a set drawn 70 percent from Second Decay material. Heldautomat released its debut single, “Am ersten Tag“, on May 15, 2026. “Anders Sein” followed on August 14, reworking a song Sippel and Purwien wrote for Second Decay’s “Taste” in 1994. “Liebe ist endlich” is the third single, and precedes the October 23 album “Zwischen den Lichtern”, produced throughout by Olaf Wollschläger and including a cover of Nine Inch Nails‘ “Hurt”. A vinyl edition of the album, limited to 100 hand-signed copies, is available alongside the digital release.

items.body: Marilyn Manson’s second studio album, “Antichrist Superstar,” turns 30 this year. The band released the record on 8 October 1996 through Nothing and Interscope Records. A rock opera and concept album, it followed 1994’s “Portrait of an American Family” and the 1995 EP “Smells Like Children,” and was recorded over roughly eight months at Nothing Studios in New Orleans. The album was produced by Marilyn Manson together with Trent Reznor, Dave Ogilvie and Sean Beavan, with Ogilvie departing partway through the sessions and Beavan brought in to finish the record with the band. Guitarist Daisy Berkowitz left the group during recording and was replaced by Zim Zum shortly after the album’s completion, with bassist Twiggy Ramirez performing the majority of the guitar parts. The 16-track CD, split into three sections titled “The Heirophant,” “Inauguration of the Worm” and “Disintegrator Rising,” runs “Irresponsible Hate Anthem,” “The Beautiful People,” “Dried Up, Tied and Dead to the World,” “Tourniquet,” “Little Horn,” “Cryptorchid,” “Deformography,” “Wormboy,” “Mister Superstar,” “Angel with the Scabbed Wings,” “Kinderfeld,” “Antichrist Superstar,” “1996,” “Minute of Decay,” “The Reflecting God” and “Man That You Fear,” followed by a hidden track, “Empty Sounds of Hate.” Album artwork was designed by P. R. Brown using photography by Dean Karr. “Antichrist Superstar” debuted at number three on the Billboard 200 and has sold close to two million copies in the United States. Lead single “The Beautiful People” preceded the album on 22 September 1996 and reached number 26 on Billboard’s Modern Rock Tracks chart and the top 20 of the UK Singles Chart, followed by second single “Tourniquet” on 8 September 1997, which peaked at number 28 in the UK. The album is the first installment of a trilogy the band completed with “Mechanical Animals” (1998) and “Holy Wood (In the Shadow of the Valley of Death)” (2000), and was supported by the year-long Dead to the World Tour. About Marilyn Manson Marilyn Manson formed in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, in 1989, when singer Brian Warner – who took the stage name Marilyn Manson – paired with guitarist Scott Putesky, known as Daisy Berkowitz. Performing initially as Marilyn Manson & the Spooky Kids, the group built a South Florida following through theatrical live shows, with a lineup that came to include bassist Brad Stewart (Gidget Gein), keyboardist Stephen Bier (Madonna Wayne Gacy) and drummer Fred Streithorst (Sara Lee Lucas). In 1993, Nine Inch Nails founder Trent Reznor signed the band as the first act on his Nothing Records label and produced their debut album, “Portrait of an American Family,” released on 19 July 1994. The “Smells Like Children” EP followed in 1995, featuring a cover of the Eurythmics’ “Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)”; Jeordie White, performing as Twiggy Ramirez, had by then replaced Gein on bass. “Antichrist Superstar” followed on 8 October 1996, co-produced by Reznor, Marilyn Manson, Dave Ogilvie and Sean Beavan, and debuted at number three on the Billboard 200 behind lead single “The Beautiful People.” The album’s success coincided with the departure of founding guitarist Daisy Berkowitz and the arrival of Zim Zum, and the band supported the record with the Dead to the World Tour. The group’s next album, “Mechanical Animals,” arrived on 15 September 1998, followed by “Holy Wood (In the Shadow of the Valley of Death)” in 2000, closing out the self-described triptych that “Antichrist Superstar” opened. Thirty years after its release, the album remains the first chapter of that trilogy.
